documents.abstract: This study investigates the reliability trap in Google Lens, an artificial intelligence-driven augmented reality translation tool. Viewing translation as human-computer interaction, this qualitative field study evaluates artificial intelligence algorithms in the Polish-to-English direction, for so-called incidental texts (text encountered in public spaces, such as signs, notices, and instructions). Analysis indicates that while neural networks deliver high grammatical fluency, their spatial context-blindness to physical geosemiotics causes severe pragmatic pitfalls affecting users, including safety, as well as legal and socio-economic risks. To address this, the paper advocates that traditional equivalence-based quality assessment must give way to a risk management paradigm. Ultimately, operating safely within the augmented linguistic landscape would entail fostering machine translation literacy and risk-aware artificial intelligence interface design.

Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for emotional and mental health support (EMS), a process in which users often described GenAI as empathic and friend-like. These descriptions suggest that people may develop imaginations of GenAI chatbots that may reflect their interpersonal needs and desires. The objective of this study is to systematically explore and thematically organizethe imaginations of GenAI among users who repeatedly use GenAI for EMS. In April 2024, we recruited 270 adults from 29 countries who had repeatedly utilized GenAI for EMS. Participants provided qualitative data regarding their imagination of ChatGPT. The analysis followed a structured reflexive thematic analysis approach. We identified two meta- themes: a) Entity (the “what”), which described the kind of beings or things they imagine GenAI as, appearing in 86.3% ( n = 233) of responses, and b) Trait (the "how"), which described users’ descriptions of perceived capacities of these beings, appearing in 36% (n = 96) of responses. The “Entity” descriptions clustered along two dimensions : abstract–concrete and human–nonhuman, which intersect to form a four-quadrant conceptual space containing 11 subthemes ranging from unbounded energy and spiritual beings to humans and robots . The “Traits” meta-theme fell into five themes: physical traits and manifestations (“looking”), cognitive abilities (“knowing”), productivity (“doing”), emotional abilities (“feeling”), and rapport (“relating”). The findings provide a systematic categorization of imaginations of GenAI for EMS, showing that GenAI is not only used as an informational tool but also imagined sometimes as an all-knowing, powerful, and highly interpersonal being. These imaginations can be highly relevant for examining human–AI relationships and underscore the need to examine how such imaginations relate to benefits and risks of AI chatbot use for mental health.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This bibliometric study maps the intersection of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and educational technologies, identifying a research gap in the lack of systematic mapping of AI engagement with human affective and cognitive factors in modern pedagogy. To address this gap, we analyzed 3,048 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus from 2015 to 2025 using the Bibliometrix R-package. We captured three thematic clusters: (1) AI integration with motivational factors, (2) human-centric elements including psychological aspects, and (3) educational technologies with a focus on learner-centered pedagogy. Centrality metrics identified “motivation” as a bridge, while the trend topic analysis revealed a growing shift toward Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). This study proposes a new conceptual framework, the AI-Mediated SLA Ecosystem, which integrates human-centric psychological dimensions as a core pillar and offers a roadmap for designing more human-centered AI learning environments.

Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

documents.abstract: Within the current European regulatory framework, in order to be authorised to perform Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) flights under the specific category of operations, applicants are required to conduct an operational risk assessment. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) selects the Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) methodology as its recommended means to perform this risk evaluation. However, some aspects of this methodology and its application are left relatively open, especially regarding the compliance with the requirements of its safety measures, called Operational Safety Objectives (OSOs). This might complicate the application of SORA, which would benefit from further guidance for its quantitative implementation. Seeking to streamline some aspects of this methodology, this paper presents the Fish Shoal Method (FSM), which combines SORA with two widespread risk analysis methods: bow-tie and Fault Tree Analysis. The synthesis of these methodologies results in a novel method that aims to provide clarity to SORA and to support applicants in the task of determining if their safety requirements are properly substantiated. The practical feasibility of FSM is demonstrated through a worked numerical example of a real UAS operation, focused on the requirements of the procedure-related OSO#08. FSM serves as a guidance to assess the performance of OSOs and make a preliminary estimation of whether the target level of safety of the operation is achieved. Since FSM formalises the main elements of SORA following a causality approach, it also allows the identification of those safety-critical items of the UAS operation that may require further attention. The outcomes of this practical example show that, even in low-risk operations, where the requirements of safety measures are less stringent, the target level of safety for OSOs aimed at human factors are too demanding from a quantitative point of view.

Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

When AI tools are used in human resource management, they can offer real-time feedback and amplify the requirement to evaluate using data. This study will investigate the potential of this mediating role between the two variables-perceived exposure to these tools and task performance for the employees-using the statistical design. There are six items in the questionnaire and the items refer to the past four weeks. There are 342 records (out of 400 submitted) that have completed answers on all 18 substantive items and are analyzed in the main analysis. Ordinary least squares regression with HC3 robust standard errors and 5,000 percentile bootstrap resample analyses results indicate a positive association of exposure to burnout (a = 0.339) and a negative association of burnout with performance (b = −0.266). The indirect effect is −0.090, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [−0.132, −0.055]. However, it has an indirect effect, which is small (0.029, p=0.515) and also has a total effect which is not significant (−0.062, p=0.161). Estimates obtained by using the alternative scoring and by covariate adjustment are similar and negative. The results indicated an indirect association of the findings to burnout that was not necessarily connected to a competitive mediation, an efficiency benefit, or causal cause. The findings suggest that focusing on employee experience is crucial when rolling out AI HR systems, in addition to their impact on performance.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

Artificial intelligence-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS) are increasingly used to inform the decisions of learners, teachers, and administrators, yet evidence on how these systems are applied, adopted, and evaluated remains fragmented. This systematic review, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, synthesized research on AI-DSS in educational settings. Searches of PubMed and Google Scholar (614 records), supplemented by 92 records identified through other methods, yielded 706 records; after deduplication and a relevance-ranked screening cap, 500 records were screened, 56 full texts were assessed, and 54 studies were included in a narrative synthesis that graded each reported outcome by the type of evidence supporting it. Six application domains were identified, led by adaptive and personalized learning and by academic performance prediction and early warning. Machine learning was the predominant approach (89% of studies), whereas explainable AI was incorporated in fewer than one quarter of studies. Adoption depended on institutional support, technical infrastructure, data quality, user-centered design, and stakeholder trust; recurrent barriers included data privacy, model opacity, algorithmic bias, implementation cost, and resistance to change. Reported benefits included more efficient assessment, earlier identification of at-risk learners, and better-informed decisions; however, comparative evidence came mainly from health-professions education, and several headline effects derived from predictive scenarios, technical reports, or single-site evaluations. Subgroup-disaggregated evidence on algorithmic equity was scarce. The review proposes an integrated decision-centered framework linking technological features, institutional conditions, human factors, and calibrated trust to appropriate use, decision quality, and educational outcomes. Advancing the field will require explainable, ethically governed, human-centered systems evaluated through longitudinal, comparative, and equity-sensitive research.

documents.abstract: Despite the widespread use of ergonomic assessment tools such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), these are typically applied on an ad-hoc basis by trained assessors and capture only a small, non-random sample of a worker's actual postural exposure. This study proposes, implements and validates a real-time, AI-based ergonomic risk assessment system that combines camera-based human pose estimation with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) data to continuously compute REBA-equivalent risk scores and to provide real-time postural-correction alerts to workers on the shop floor of a medium-scale manufacturing company in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The framework was deployed with 42 assembly-line workers in a mid-sized discrete-manufacturing facility over a 10-week period (4 weeks baseline, 6 weeks intervention), and the AI-generated risk scores were compared against masked manual REBA scores obtained by two certified ergonomists. The AI system achieved 89.6% overall agreement with the manual assessment (weighted kappa = 0.85) and a strong correlation with manual scores (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). The mean weekly REBA score fell from 6.95 to 4.80, and the number of high-risk posture events fell from about 18.5 to 6.5 events per worker-shift, while self-reported musculoskeletal discomfort on the Standardised Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire decreased across all six body regions measured, particularly the lower back (51.3% to 35.7%) and shoulders (44.2% to 31.5%). The results suggest that sensor-fused AI-based ergonomic monitoring can significantly enhance the scalability and objectivity of postural risk surveillance relative to periodic manual assessment, and that when combined with real-time worker-facing feedback, it can measurably lower biomechanical risk exposure and self-reported discomfort within a single production quarter.

documents.abstract: Ensuring high levels of Situation awareness (SA) is essential for air traffic controllers (ATCOs), enabling them to continuously process and integrate information into a comprehensive understanding of the situation as it dynamically changes. In the context of human-automation collaboration, SA becomes even more critical, as operators must be prepared to take over control in emergency situations. Although existing studies have largely assessed SA as either poor or good, limited research has explored identification of SA levels (Level 1, 2, and 3). To investigate the potential of eye-tracking technology for real-time SA levels assessment, we conducted an SA-inducing experiment involving 18 participants. Participants are required to perform a series of air traffic control (ATC) tasks corresponding to three SA levels, while their eye-tracking data were simultaneously collected. Eye-tracking features are analyzed using a two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Results identified total fixation duration, number of fixations, average pupil diameter and average amplitude of saccades as key indicators for distinguishing SA levels. Additionally, our findings highlight a significant interaction between SA levels and workload, demonstrating that the effectiveness of these metrics varies under different workload conditions. These insights contribute to enhancing real-time SA evaluation in the safety-critical environments like ATC, further improving the overall operational efficiency and safety in various human-automation collaboration scenarios.

Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

documents.abstract: Automation, digitalization, and, more recently, generative artificial intelligence (gAI) are changing the skill sets employers demand. However, understanding remains limited about how different sector-level stakeholders in developing countries perceive these innovations, and about these technologies' impact on university graduates' employability. The comparative qualitative study draws on 60 interviews with graduates, employer representatives and academics, five of each type per sector, in four Bangladeshi sectors (readymade garments and textiles (RMG); information and communication technology and IT-enabled services (ICT/ITES); banking and financial services; logistics and supply chain management), as well as multi-sector comparative data. Reflexive thematic analysis yielded cross-sector themes, which include framing of technology and specific discussion of AI in ICT/ITES, disciplinary expertise being necessary but no longer sufficient, with digital, data and adaptive capabilities increasingly essential and learned largely outside formal programmes, cross-sector problems with institutional coordination due to curricula lag (the mode and extent of lag varies according to discipline), reasons why these results should not be taken as an indication of job loss and the impact of gAI, as well as sector-specific and generic implications for universities, sectors and employer associations with clear links to the data. Shortcomings include reliance on perceptions, small cell sizes across multiple parameters, and a lack of a worker perspective.

documents.abstract: Background: AI systems are increasingly deployed to support mental health clinicians, yet real-world evidence remains limited. In crisis counseling, where clients often seek human connection, understanding whether AI augmentation preserves or undermines meaningful human engagement is essential. Methods: In a mixed-methods study of a counselor-facing AI copilot on a WhatsApp-based crisis hotline in India (Mar.-Oct. 2025), counselors could request, edit, and send AI messages. We analyzed 20 interviews, 8 shadowing sessions, 56 survey responses, and edits in 27,778 copilot messages from 108 counselors via thematic analysis (Technology Acceptance Model 2, plus inductive coding of emergent factors), and survey statistics. Results: Counselors reported high copilot acceptance (survey): 98.2% found it helpful; 89.3% likely to continue use; 80.4% reported efficiency gains. Interviews highlighted sentence scaffolding, empathetic phrasing, stress reduction, catching missed details, and efficiency. Barriers (survey) included repetitive outputs (23.2%), lack of context (17.9%), and authenticity concerns (10.7%). While 69.6% (survey) reported skill enhancement, interviews surfaced skill atrophy concerns. Counselors frequently accepted copilot suggestions, editing to remove questions, adjust tone, or personalize style. Conclusion: In one of the largest real-world deployments of a counselor-facing mental health AI copilot, counselors reported reduced cognitive load, empathetic communication, and greater efficiency, alongside concerns about skill atrophy, authenticity, and over-reliance. In settings like crisis counseling where clients seek human connection, AI tools must balance operational support with preserving clinical skill and genuine therapeutic engagement. Designs soliciting approval or editing of complete drafts may overweight efficiency at the expense of sustained human engagement.

documents.abstract: As higher education increasingly adopts transdisciplinary frameworks to address complex societal challenges, cultivating students’ higher-order thinking (HOT) skills has become a key educational goal. These cognitive processes are essential in Human Factors Engineering (HFE), which requires students to address wicked problems inherent in transdisciplinary human-technology systems. However, traditional HFE curricula often emphasise rote memorisation of scientific theories. Meanwhile, the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has altered how students engage with academic content by enabling instant access to AI-generated responses. Despite increasing interest in AI-assisted learning, empirical evidence examining LLMs as co-creative partners in activities designed to support HOT remains limited. This quasi-experimental study compares two cohorts in an undergraduate HFE course, in which students either generated exam questions independently or co-created questions with an LLM. A total of 166 multiple-choice questions were collected and classified according to Bloom’s Taxonomy by two independent raters. Results indicate that the LLM-collaboration group produced a significantly higher proportion of higher-order questions. Among student-level factors, the number of student-AI dialogue turns was associated with question cognitive level, whereas self-reported AI usage frequency, metacognitive awareness and prior AI experience were not. Additionally, whether students adopted the AI’s suggested question or wrote their own after the dialogue did not affect question cognitive level. An exploratory analysis suggested that the number of turns in which students critically engaged with AI outputs was marginally associated with higher question cognitive level. These findings highlight the potential value of student-AI dialogue logs as a complementary source of assessment evidence.

Complex 3D environments like Blender present a steep learning curve for novices, where topological errors often remain hidden until the final stages of a project. From a Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) perspective, supporting these users means moving away from static tutorials and toward active, real-time guidance. To explore this, we introduce “Learn & Fix,” a functional prototype Blender add-on with a rule-based architecture that detects mesh flaws in real time and helps new users by explaining their mistakes. We conducted a formative usability pilot study (N = 8) with absolute beginner users (less than 20 h of use) to evaluate interface discoverability, perceived usefulness, and interaction friction. Questionnaire responses highlighted an onboarding discoverability issue, as testers struggled to start the add-on in Blender’s native UI. User feedback indicates that in-viewport validation helps learners spot structural errors early. The design of an educational add-on must balance native UI integration with clear visibility.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to conceptualise a Three-Level Cognitive Cross-Pollination Model involving AI Developers and Controllers, Industry Application Integrators, and AI Beneficiaries in a hypothetical future Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) society. It seeks to explore multidirectional knowledge exchange, stakeholder collaboration, and governance mechanisms to promote responsible AI innovation, equitable benefit distribution, and sustainable human-centred societal development. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory, qualitative, literature-based conceptual research approach, drawing upon secondary sources to examine cognitive cross-pollination among three stakeholder groups in a hypothetical future AGI and ASI society. It employs SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, qualitative predictive scenario analysis, and impact analysis to evaluate the proposed model's technological, organisational, ethical, economic, and societal implications. Analysis/Result: The integrated SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, predictive scenario, and impact analyses highlight the potential strengths, opportunities, benefits, constraints, and challenges of cognitive cross-pollination among the three stakeholder groups in a future AGI and ASI society. The findings suggest that multidirectional knowledge exchange, stakeholder collaboration, continuous feedback, and responsible governance could promote technological innovation, industrial integration, equitable benefit distribution, and sustainable human-centred societal development. Originality/Value: This study proposes a novel Three-Level Cognitive Cross-Pollination Model that integrates AI Developers and Controllers, Industry Application Integrators, and AI Beneficiaries into a unified conceptual framework for a hypothetical future AGI and ASI society. Its originality lies in examining multidirectional knowledge exchange and stakeholder interdependence through integrated SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, predictive scenario, and impact analyses, offering valuable insights into responsible AI governance, collaborative innovation, and sustainable human-centred development. Type of Paper: Exploratory Research Analysis

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make introductory programming tasks easier to complete, but a working program is not evidence of durable learning. This conceptual-theoretical paper integrates research on cognitive load, metacognition, self-explanation, productive failure, appropriate reliance on automation, and recent studies of AI-assisted programming to propose a five-phase cognitive-scaffolding framework. Learners first make an unaided attempt, request bounded assistance, verify the response against requirements and independently designed tests, explain the mechanism and calibrate confidence, and then complete a related transfer task as support fades. AI literacy, ethical disclosure, privacy, and instructor orchestration operate across all phases. The framework identifies process evidence that remains inspectable when generated code is available, including problem representations, hypotheses, verification records, explanations, confidence judgments, and unaided transfer. It also states six testable propositions and an evaluation blueprint for introductory programming courses. The contribution is a bounded design logic, not a claim that the sequence has already been validated: GenAI should reduce avoidable burden while leaving consequential decisions, checks, and explanations with the learner.

documents.abstract: The development of students’ visual–spatial reasoning is a persistent challenge in geometry learning, where abstract representations and spatial transformations require high levels of cognitive engagement. Although flipped learning has been widely implemented to promote active learning, its effectiveness largely depends on the quality of instructional design and pedagogical support provided during in-class activities. This study investigates how metacognitive scaffolding can be intentionally designed and embedded within flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed in secondary geometry instruction involving 62 students assigned to experimental and control groups. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-tests of visual–spatial reasoning, while qualitative data were obtained from classroom observations and semi-structured teacher interviews. The results indicate that students who experienced metacognitive scaffolding within a flipped learning environment demonstrated significantly greater gains in visual–spatial reasoning than those in a conventional flipped classroom, with a large effect size. Qualitative findings further reveal that scaffolding prompts supported students’ planning, monitoring, and reflective evaluation during problem-solving activities. Overall, the findings suggest that flipped learning environments become more cognitively productive when structured metacognitive scaffolding is deliberately incorporated into the learning design.

Introduction Society 5.0 integrates advanced digital technologies with human-centered work systems, yet its implications for sustainable employee performance remain underexplored. Drawing on Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examines the relationship between Society 5.0 enablement intensity (S5EI) and sustainable human performance through autonomous motivation and emotional exhaustion, considering human-centric governance capability as a moderator. Methods The study employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyse data collected from 519 employees working in digitally intensive sectors in India. Results The findings indicate that S5EI is positively associated with sustainable human performance, primarily through autonomous motivation. Emotional exhaustion partially offsets this positive effect through competitive mediation. Human-centric governance capability strengthens the relationship between autonomous motivation and sustainable human performance but does not significantly buffer the negative effect of emotional exhaustion. Discussion The findings conceptualize digital enablement as a dual-valence work condition that simultaneously strengthens autonomy-based motivation and increases digital demands, integrating Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of participatory digital governance, workload management, and employee recovery measures for supporting sustainable human performance.

Organizations navigating digital transformation face persistent challenges integrating social and technical elements to support innovation and worker wellbeing. Despite increasing workforce participation, women remain underrepresented in senior leadership roles that shape how this integration occurs, leaving perspectives shaped by gendered organizational experience underexplored within digital transformation research. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with sixteen senior women leaders across Australian organizations, this study applies socio‐technical systems theory and a gender‐informed leadership perspective to examine how these leaders understood and navigated the relationship between technical and social domains during digital transformation. Participants treated technical and social considerations as mutually constitutive, enacting their integration through communication, employee participation, human‐centered work design, capability development and ongoing adaptation. Psychosocial safety emerged across technical, social and integration‐focused accounts as a system‐level condition implicated in this process. Together, these findings provide an empirical account of human‐centric transformation within Industry 5.0 and extend socio‐technical systems theory by conceptualizing integration as an enacted process through which technical and social considerations continually shape one another. A gender‐informed analysis further demonstrates the value of gendered organizational experience for understanding how socio‐technical integration is accomplished in practice.

The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study investigated the effect of facilitated Problem-Based Learning (PBL) on intrinsic and extrinsic motivation among nursing students in North-East Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design was adopted. The population comprised 1,065 ND II nursing students from six Colleges of Nursing Science in North-East Nigeria, from which 200 students were selected using a multi-stage sampling procedure. The sample consisted of 100 students in the experimental group exposed to facilitated PBL and 100 students in the control group taught using conventional lecture-based instruction. Data were collected using a 28-item Academic Motivation Questionnaire (AMQ). The instrument demonstrated satisfactory reliability with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.84. The experimental group participated in a six-week facilitated PBL intervention involving nursing-related case scenarios, guided questioning, collaborative learning, feedback, and self-directed learning activities. Data were analyzed using means, standard deviations, and t-tests at the 0.05 level of significance. Finding showed that the experimental group recorded an increase in mean intrinsic-motivation scores from 26.30 at pre-test to 50.30 at post-test, compared with an increase from 25.90 to 30.20 in the control group. A significant effect was also found on extrinsic motivation, with the experimental group recording a greater reduction in extrinsic motivation than the control group, t(198) = 8.72, p < .05. therefore, motivation also differed significantly between the facilitated PBL and lecture groups, t(198) = 14.02, p < .001. Furthermore, a significant difference was observed between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, t(198) = 6.85, p < .001. The study concluded that facilitated PBL is an effective instructional approach for strengthening intrinsic motivation and promoting more self-directed learning among nursing students. It was recommended that nursing institutions should integrate facilitated PBL into their programmes, train educators in effective PBL facilitation, provide adequate learning resources, and emphasize learning activities that foster students’ intrinsic motivation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents are entering administrative processes. This marks a shift from robotic process automation to intelligent automation and raises the question of what role people keep when systems process, analyze, and make decisions. The objective was to critically analyze the literature from 2020 to 2026 on the competencies that are transformed or emerging, and on research trends and gaps. A critical and integrative documentary study was carried out in Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, Redalyc, Dialnet, and Google Scholar. It included peer-reviewed studies in Spanish and English, which were analyzed with an extraction matrix and a thematic synthesis. Based on the reviewed literature, GenAI cuts writing time by up to 40% and raises productivity by 15%, especially among novices. However, greater trust in it reduces critical thinking. The emerging competencies are data analysis, digital and complex cognitive skills, decision-making, and continuous learning. Qualitative and short-term studies predominate. There are gaps in the quality of oversight, in Latin American contexts, SMEs, and the public sector, and in the development of expertise. The human role is shifting from execution to oversight and governance. It is effective only under adequate conditions and complying with a protocol is not enough.

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation, remote and hybrid work, and the diffusion of artificial intelligence have made employee adaptability a critical organizational capability, yet research on its antecedents remains fragmented across psychology, information systems, and management. This study aims to synthesize evidence on the individual and organizational determinants of employee adaptability in the digital workplace. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and ABI/INFORM for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025, and findings were integrated through thematic synthesis. The review shows that adaptability is conceptualized as a multidimensional capability spanning cognitive, behavioral, and emotional responses to technological change. Individual determinants include dispositional traits, self-efficacy and digital competence, career adaptability, and attitudes toward change, whereas organizational determinants include leadership and change communication, psychological safety, training, job and technology design, and flexible work arrangements. The literature suggests that these determinants operate as interacting resources, with supportive organizational conditions amplifying individual capacity. An integrative framework and a research agenda emphasizing longitudinal, multilevel, and emerging-economy studies are proposed. The findings guide managers and human resource practitioners in designing workplaces that support adaptation.

Vertical farming (VF) represents a transformative approach to agricultural production utilizing multi-tiered, controlled-environment systems, yet it introduces unique ergonomic challenges distinct from conventional agriculture. This literature review synthesizes current evidence on ergonomic issues in vertical farming systems, alongside evidence from indoor farming and broader controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) systems, examining musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) prevalence, risk factors, assessment methodologies, and intervention strategies. Agricultural workers in greenhouse and indoor farming environments experience MSD prevalence rates of 50.9% to 89.3%, with the lower back, shoulders, knees, and neck most commonly affected. Available evidence suggests that vertical farming may present distinctive ergonomic challenges, including multi-tiered configurations associated with overhead reaching, lower-tier access constraints, repetitive precision tasks, environmental stressors, and complex human-technology interactions. However, much of the current evidence is inferred from greenhouse and broader controlled-environment agriculture systems. While traditional ergonomic assessment tools (RULA, REBA, OWAS) and advanced methods (EMG) have been applied in agricultural contexts, their adaptation to vertical farming remains limited. Current interventions show promise through workspace optimization, tool redesign, automation, and participatory ergonomics approaches. However, significant knowledge gaps persist regarding longitudinal health outcomes, human-automation interaction, cognitive ergonomics, and socioeconomic dimensions specific to vertical farming. This review highlights the emerging need for human-centered design principles in VF system development to ensure worker health, safety, and operational sustainability.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In industrialized countries, rapid population aging and declining birth rates have made labor shortages a critical issue in industrial workplaces. Without actively utilizing elderly workers, persons with disabilities, and foreign workers, on-site operations risk becoming unsustainable. Addressing this challenge requires not only technological innovation but also a transdisciplinary engineering approach that integrates human, social, and industrial system perspectives. This study proposes a personalized work design framework that combines generative artificial intelligence (AI) and ergonomics to enable inclusive and sustainable industrial operations. The proposed framework utilizes individual attribute data—such as age-related physical characteristics, functional limitations, work experience, and language proficiency—to generate task configurations tailored to diverse worker groups. Ergonomic principles are systematically embedded into the generative AI model to adapt task sequences, work postures, workload distribution, and operational instructions according to individual capabilities and constraints. From an engineering perspective, the framework integrates data-driven AI modeling, human factors engineering, and production system design to dynamically optimize the interaction between workers and industrial environments. A case study conducted in a manufacturing-related setting demonstrates that the proposed approach reduces physical strain and cognitive workload while maintaining or improving productivity and operational stability. The results indicate that AI-driven ergonomic task personalization is particularly effective in enabling the participation of elderly workers, persons with disabilities, and foreign workers in on-site industrial work. This research highlights the value of transdisciplinary engineering in addressing complex societal challenges posed by demographic change. By bridging generative AI, ergonomics, and industrial engineering, the proposed framework provides a scalable and human-centered solution for designing adaptive workplaces and supporting long-term workforce sustainability in aging and diversifying societies.

This article reports on an empirical study conducted among a cohort of pre-service teachers, aimed at enhancing their professional competencies within a university teacher training institute. Grounded in the theoretical and methodological framework of professional didactics, this research investigates how analyzing professional situations contributes to skill acquisition and psychological well-being. The variables measured throughout this inquiry include classroom management skills, individual reflective capacity, and situational stress perceived by the participants. The quantitative and qualitative findings reveal a statistically weak correlation between reflexivity and the development of professional competencies. Crucially, the data demonstrate no significant relationship between a teacher's reflective capacity and their level of perceived situational stress. These results suggest that while fostering reflexivity helps to enhance professional competencies and pedagogical reasoning, it is inherently insufficient to reduce the psychological burden and stress experienced by novice teachers in the classroom. Consequently, this study argues that professional training frameworks cannot rely solely on reflexive analysis to ensure occupational health. To bridge this gap, teacher education programs would significantly benefit from integrating explicit stress management practices, emotional regulation techniques, and coping strategies directly into their core curricula. By doing so, training institutes could offer a more holistic approach, combining cognitive professional development with the psychological resilience necessary for sustainable teaching careers.

Purpose This study examines how organizations construct governance responses to externally driven volatility by embedding external signals into control practices. Focusing on climate exposed agricultural firms, this study extends dynamic capabilities theory (DCT) by developing external resilience controls (ERCs) as a sociotechnical governance construct that illuminates how firms make volatility actionable through formal control routines. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a pragmatic constructivist design science orientation, this study combines six years of financial and operational context (2019–2024) with a longitudinal interpretive content analysis of annual report and sustainability disclosures (2022–2024) from five major agricultural firms. An interpretive design approach enables the systematic synthesis of disclosed organizational practices into a conceptual framework. Findings ERCs emerge as sociotechnical governance arrangements that translate external volatility into organizationally meaningful routines and actionable dynamic capabilities. These arrangements materialize through digital sensing infrastructures, traceability systems, scenario thresholds and board-level oversight that collectively shape how firms interpret and respond to climate anomalies, regulatory shifts and technological change. ERCs reveal resilience as an ongoing process of constructing, stabilizing and legitimizing responses to external volatility. Practical implications ERCs offer practitioners an analytic framework to operationalize dynamic capabilities by integrating digital tools and governance structures. They show how firms convert external volatility into actionable sensing, seizing and reconfiguring routines, enabling adaptive decision-making without relying on rigid control mechanisms. Originality/value This study advances qualitative management scholarship by conceptualizing ERCs as sociotechnical governance constructs. It contributes to strategy research by extending DCT, showing how dynamic capabilities are enacted through the interplay of digital infrastructures, institutional pressures, and organizational sensemaking.

This article analyzes the Knowledge Lighthouse, the name Petrobras gives to the knowledge management practice commonly known as Yellow Pages. The solution is a business intelligence dashboard that integrates corporate data and professional records to locate expertise by knowledge area or by person. A qualitative and descriptive approach was adopted through a single case study and bibliographic and documentary analysis. The theoretical framework combines knowledge management, transactive memory, competence mapping, intellectual capital, communities of practice, and sociotechnical systems. The study describes the dashboard’s conception, its SAP/SIRH data sources, daily D-1 updating, search and profile detail views, query paths, and corporate access. The analytical findings indicate that the solution may improve expert findability, reduce search costs, foster learning and knowledge integration, and support critical knowledge management, team formation, innovation, internal mobility, succession, and organizational memory. Its effectiveness, however, depends on a governed taxonomy, complete and current data, trust, participation, workflow integration, data protection, and value-oriented evaluation. The study concludes that the Knowledge Lighthouse should operate as an infrastructure for discovery and connection, complemented by human validation and linked to communities, repositories, and knowledgetransfer practices, rather than being converted into an automatic employee assessment mechanism.

documents.abstract: Healthcare Facility Management depends on information distributed across Building Information Models (BIMs), operational sensor systems, and multiple organizational actors, yet the transition from BIM-organized asset representation to a decision-supporting, Digital-Twin-enabled environment remains insufficiently operationalized. This study develops and instantiates a management-oriented framework for this transition through a literature-informed, case-derived design at a complex hospital surgical department. Evidence was classified by maturity level and cross-mapped across six information-and-decision layers: Asset Information, Operational Data, Integration and Information Management, Facility Management Process, Decision Support, and Organizational and Governance. The framework was instantiated against two documented prototype-level sensor subsystems. The scientific contribution is a traceable mapping from case evidence and literature requirements to six information-and-decision layers, making the boundary between demonstrated outputs and unobserved human action explicit. The managerial contribution is a cross-layer requirement matrix and a five-phase roadmap with auditable progression gates, linking each information requirement to a responsible role and a maintenance decision. The evidence comprises a documented information environment, functioning sensor prototypes, and integration tested in a virtual environment with real sensor data. The framework offers healthcare Facility Management practitioners a planning instrument for preparing and assessing the transition; practitioner assessment, multi-case testing, and longitudinal hospital deployment are its next validation stages.

Purpose The main objective is to analyze the sociotechnical implications of Artificial Intelligence as it transitions from an assistive model (“copilot”) to an agentic and autonomous model. It seeks to explore how this new environment redefines human identity, authorship, and the autonomy of thought in the face of total technical integration. Method The study employs a theoretical-critical analysis methodology based on Media Ecology as a metadiscipline. It adopts a systemic and longitudinal perspective that traces the evolution of human interfaces from the control of fire to the present. As a primary diagnostic tool, it uses the McLuhan Tetrad to examine what AI enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into. Findings AI as an Exocortex: AI functions as an external layer of brain processing that tends to reshape our decisions, tastes, and analyses. Autonomous and Agentic Model: Unlike previous media that functioned as a human reflection, AI contributes to creating an autonomous model capable of generating culture and narratives independently. The “Black Box” Effect: The inscrutable nature of neural networks hinders transparency and oversight in critical areas like justice or healthcare. Displacement of Judgment: There is a progressive “anesthesia” where human critical judgment is displaced toward automated algorithmic processes. Implications Cognitive Amputation: By delegating decision-making and technical labor to machines, humans risk the atrophy of their own critical and creative capacities. Crisis of Truth: AI can “hack” the operating system of civilization (language), creating “reality bubbles” where “truth” becomes a byproduct of the algorithm rather than human dialectics. Dictatorship of Efficiency: The velocity of AI exceeds the response capacity of democratic institutions, potentially rendering “freedom of choice” an obsolete concept in favor of automated efficiency. Value The text provides a critical outlook that moves beyond technical optimism, proposing an “ethics of selective disconnection”. Its value lies in defending human imperfection, ambiguity, and silence as essential non-optimizable elements that must be preserved against the binary logic of AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital labour platforms increasingly organise work through algorithmic systems that allocate tasks, monitor performance, determine access to income-generating opportunities, calculate remuneration, and impose sanctions. These systems may reduce coordination costs and expand market access, yet they also create distinctive problems of wage justice when workers cannot understand the rules governing earnings, verify deductions, contest adverse decisions, or identify the institution responsible for algorithmic outcomes. This article develops a critical-conceptual framework that reconstructs the Islamic concept of ujrāh for the governance of remuneration in the platform economy. It integrates scholarship on algorithmic management and platform labour, organisational justice, labour regulation, and Islamic jurisprudence on ijārah and ethical remuneration. The analysis proceeds through conceptual mapping, normative interpretation, institutional translation, and framework synthesis. It argues that ujrāh should not be confined to the nominal amount agreed for a task; its contemporary ethical assessment must also encompass the procedures and infrastructures through which work is allocated, remuneration is calculated, and payment rights are enforced. The article proposes five interdependent dimensions of Islamic algorithmic wage justice: distributive fairness; contractual intelligibility; algorithmic explainability and contestability; equitable allocation of economic risk; and protection of human dignity and worker agency. The framework contributes to platform-work scholarship by connecting distributive and procedural justice with a normative account of contractual responsibility grounded in Islamic economic ethics. It is conceptual and requires empirical testing across platform sectors and regulatory settings.

As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

This article examines Jiacan, Chinese food‐delivery riders' term for retaining or consuming undelivered food. Drawing on digital ethnography of rider chat groups, interviews, Douyin vlogs and public discussion threads, it shows how grievance‐linked Jiacan acquires resistant meaning through customer‐mediated disputes, digital circulation and peer evaluation. We develop Gamified Resistance to describe resistance socially organised through shared procedures, risk–reward calculations and judgments about acceptable conduct. The analysis identifies three pathways through which resistance may reproduce platform control: proceduralised rule‐navigation, triadic displacement toward customers and priced dissent. Riders can obtain immediate relief or retaliation while sustaining dependence on platform adjudication, customer‐mediated relations and sanctions. Control reproduction remains provisional: peer judgments, public scrutiny and customer claims can regulate participation and channel disputes, but also challenge the practice or redirect conflict toward the platform.

Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

Aligning human capabilities with system requirements is crucial for lowering injury risks and enhancing performance in industrial settings like the assembly of automobiles. In this context, we define the Ergodesign Framework as a structure for integrating ergonomics and its findings, Ergodesign and its generation of principles, and design and its pursuit of technical solutions within a transdisciplinary, continuous, and bidirectional process. In this paper, we focus on the internal Ergodesign process, whose objective is to translate ergonomic data into design-relevant principles that can subsequently be applied during design phases, thereby enabling the proactive implementation of ergonomic requirements. The process is based on the capitalization of recurring issues observed during ergonomic analyses, the identification of their root causes, and the definition of Ergodesign rules, making it possible to create a database of Ergodesign principles that can be applied by designers. This process is implemented within the company Lohr Industrie, where standardized elements were developed to define internal rules for product and process design, based on findings from ergonomic studies conducted across different workshops. Through this application, the process of translating ergonomic data into design-relevant principles via Ergodesign emerges as a central component of the Ergodesign Framework.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are promoted as the technological backbone of Industry 5.0, which re-centres manufacturing on human well-being, resilience, and sustainability. This PRISMA 2020-guided review combines bibliometric analysis with narrative synthesis to examine how the human and ethical dimensions of AI- and IoT-driven smart manufacturing are addressed. Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore searches without a start-year limit identified 1904 unique records; all were coded at abstract level (647 eligible records), and 86 prioritized records were synthesized in full text around five research questions: ethical risk, human factors, operationalization of human-centricity, governance, and the technology-readiness gap. Performance, thematic-evolution, co-citation, usage, and readership analyses complement the synthesis. Human-factors and architecture research dominate, yet reviews and conceptual papers prevail, and only 10% of eligible records report industrial validation. Ethical risk is the fastest-growing theme but is operationalized mainly as explainability. Governance is the primary object of 2.8% of eligible records, and its intellectual base is thin: about 3% of these studies cite the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or AI-law scholarship. A human-centric Industry 5.0 maturity model and a research agenda are proposed.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
